title: Tenali Raman and the Royal Brinjal Curry

full_text:
In the private gardens of the palace of Vijayanagara, the royal horticulturists had cultivated a rare, experimental variety of purple brinjal (eggplant). The fruit was sweet, succulent, and had a delicate aroma found nowhere else in the kingdom.
King Krishnadevaraya was so fond of this vegetable that he declared it exclusive to the royal table, decreeing that anyone who stole or cultivated it without permission would face severe punishment.

One evening, after dining with the King, Tenali was given a small portion of the royal brinjal curry to take home.
His wife, Sharada, tasted the curry and found it sublime. She begged Tenali:
'Raman, our young son has never tasted such a delicacy! You are a favorite of the King; surely you can bring a single brinjal from the garden for our child?'

Tenali was reluctant, but moved by fatherly affection, he slipped into the garden at twilight and plucked one ripe purple brinjal.
Sharada prepared a delicious curry and served it to their little son, who ate it with joyful praise.

However, Tenali realized the danger: children are innocent and often speak the truth without thinking. If the boy mentioned the royal brinjal to the neighbors or schoolmates, disaster would strike the family!

Tenali devised an ingenious psychological plan.
That night, while the child was sleeping deeply, Tenali carried him up to the terrace roof.
Tenali and his wife took buckets of cool water and poured them gently over the roof tiles, splashing the sleeping boy.
Then Tenali flashed a polished brass tray before a lamp to simulate lightning, while Sharada rolled a heavy brass pestle across the floor to mimic the rumble of thunder!
Tenali gently shook the boy awake, shouting:
'Wake up, son! A terrifying midnight thunderstorm has struck the city! Rain is pouring through the roof! Eat this piece of sweet brinjal curry for strength, and let us hurry downstairs before the lightning strikes!'
The bewildered, sleepy child ate the morsel, saw the water splashing, heard the thunder, and was tucked back into bed.

The next day, the royal gardener noticed a missing brinjal and reported the theft. Suspicion fell upon Tenali, whose love for good food was well known.
The King summoned Tenali and his young son to court.
The King asked the boy gently: 'Little one, did your father bring you a special purple brinjal from the royal garden for dinner yesterday?'

The boy replied eagerly:
'Yes, Maharaj! We ate it at midnight during the great thunderstorm, when lightning flashed through our bedroom and rain flooded our roof!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the ministers stared at the boy, then looked outside at the bright, dry sky.
The King laughed:
'Yesterday was a clear, dry summer night without a single cloud or drop of rain in all of Vijayanagara! The poor child was having a wild, imaginative nightmare!'

The King dismissed the accusation with affectionate chuckles.
Tenali bowed gratefully, having protected his family while leaving the court in good humor, proving that foresight and wit can defuse the greatest perils.
moral: Quick wit and psychological understanding can rescue a loved one from harsh royal wrath.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Brinjal Curry"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
